blocks.hero_h1: Toyota Land Cruiser Prado 2002 Import NZ
blocks.hero_subtitle: The 2002 Prado is useful to understand properly, because October 2002 marked the move into the J120 generation. We check whether you are looking at a late earlier car or a 120 Series vehicle, then confirm the exact engine, grade and auction-list details before bidding, so you are not paying for the wrong generation or stepping into avoidable compliance uncertainty.
proof_points: Importing estimate, with compliance as part of the process
blocks.why_kiwis_buy: People look at the Prado because it is a proper body-on-frame Toyota SUV with full-time 4WD rather than a soft-roader setup. The 120 Series also brought the newer 1KD-FTV common-rail diesel, which matters because it was the newer diesel option at launch while the petrol 3RZ-FE and 5VZ-FE carried over from the earlier Prado. For buyers who want one vehicle for daily use, towing and rougher roads, that mix is a big part of the appeal.
blocks.video_caption: A Prado makes sense when you need one vehicle to cover family use, towing and rougher roads without getting too complicated. On this shape, the long-wheelbase 5-door body is 4715mm long with a 2790mm wheelbase, so it has the footprint buyers expect from a genuine medium-large 4WD.
blocks.main_usp_deep: The big draw with a 2002 Prado is not one single trim, it is the combination of Toyota 4WD hardware and a wide spread of usable engine choices. On J120 models, full-time 4WD came with a 2-speed transfer and a Torsen centre differential with centre diff lock. That setup gives you constant drive to all four wheels, then low range and a lockable centre diff when the surface gets loose or you are pulling weight. It is also one of those model lines where getting the exact chassis code right matters, because 2002 spans two Prado generations.

buyer_persona.headline: Who is this car right for?
buyer_persona.body: This suits buyers who want a genuine 4WD Toyota for towing, family trips or rural use, and who understand that a 2002 vehicle needs careful selection rather than assumptions. It also works for buyers who want the newer-shape 120 Series specifically and are happy for us to confirm the exact engine, grade and auction-list notes first. If you want a dependable daily SUV with proper 4WD ability rather than just a tall wagon, it is a solid match.

car_specs_benefits.spec: J120 Series production: Oct 2002 to Aug 2009
car_specs_benefits.benefit: That date split matters because a 2002 Prado can be either the earlier shape or the newer 120 Series, so checking the model code avoids buying the wrong generation.
You get constant four-wheel drive on road, then low range when you need slower, more controlled pulling power.

car_specs_benefits.spec: Torsen centre differential with centre diff lock
car_specs_benefits.benefit: This is a proper mechanical 4WD setup, not just an on-demand system, and the lock function helps when grip is uneven from side to side.

car_specs_benefits.spec: Engine options: 3RZ-FE 2.7 petrol 120kW, 5VZ-FE 3.4 V6 petrol 136kW, 1KD-FTV 3.0 turbo-diesel 120kW
car_specs_benefits.benefit: There is a clear choice between simpler petrol ownership, smoother V6 power, or the newer common-rail diesel depending on how you plan to use it.
You can target a shorter-wheelbase truck for tighter use or the longer 5-door for family space and touring practicality.

standout_features_block.headline: Features that stand out
standout_features_block.intro: On a Prado of this age, the worthwhile features are the ones that change how it works day to day, not the usual basic equipment list.

items.title: 3-door or 5-door body choice
items.body: This generation was offered in both 3-door and 5-door form. The shorter body gives you a 2455mm wheelbase, while the 5-door stretches to 2790mm, so the choice changes parking ease, rear-seat access and touring space in a real way.

items.title: TX Limited grade in the range
items.body: TX Limited sits above the regular TX in the grade ladder, which is useful because it gives buyers a known higher-spec version to target when scanning auction cars. Exact equipment still needs confirming on the individual vehicle, but it is one of the trims worth understanding before you bid.
items.image_hint: Rear badge or side exterior shot where the grade emblem is visible

items.title: Long-wheelbase 5-door dimensions
items.body: The 5-door body measures 4715mm long and 1875mm wide, which puts it in the proper family-4WD bracket rather than compact-SUV territory. That extra length is part of why the Prado has remained popular with buyers who need one vehicle to do several jobs.
items.image_hint: Three-quarter exterior shot showing the full length and upright SUV shape

items.title: Short-wheelbase 3-door option
items.body: The 3-door version is 4340mm long, so it is meaningfully shorter than the 5-door. That is a useful detail if you want Prado running gear and 4WD hardware without the full-size footprint.
items.image_hint: Compact 3-door Prado parked in a tighter urban space to show the shorter body

tech_deep_dive_block.headline: Under the skin
tech_deep_dive_block.intro: The Prado earns its reputation from the hardware underneath it, and this is the part worth understanding before choosing an engine or body style.

items.title: Full-time 4WD with Torsen centre differential
items.body: The J120 Prado used full-time 4WD rather than a part-time setup. A Torsen centre differential manages the front-to-rear drive split in normal use, then the centre diff lock can mechanically tie the axles together when the surface gets slippery. That gives the Prado a more settled feel on sealed roads than an old-school part-time system, because you are not switching between 2WD and 4WD. It is one of the practical reasons these work well as everyday SUVs as well as weekend tow or track vehicles.

items.title: 2-speed transfer case
items.body: The transfer case gives you high range for normal driving and low range for slower, heavier work. Low range is not about speed, it is about control, especially when climbing, descending or pulling a load at low pace. Buyers who only look at engine size sometimes miss this, but the transfer case is a big part of what separates a Prado from a road-focused SUV. If you need a genuine 4WD tool, this matters more than a long options list.

items.title: Engine range at launch
items.body: The launch-era engine lineup covered three quite different buyers. The 3RZ-FE 2.7-litre petrol made 120kW, the 5VZ-FE 3.4-litre V6 made 136kW, and the 1KD-FTV 3.0-litre turbo-diesel made 120kW. The useful point here is that the diesel was the newer D-4D common-rail option for the 120 Series, while the petrol engines carried over from the earlier Prado. On an import search, that helps narrow the kind of Prado you actually want.

items.title: Model range split in 2002
items.body: This is one of those years where the production split matters as much as the badge. Early 2002 vehicles can still be the earlier Prado generation, while October 2002 marks the start of the J120 series. If you are aiming for the newer platform, checking the model code first is one of the simplest ways to avoid paying for the wrong vehicle.
